Python instructions to handle a named kind of exception.
The Python exception for trying to access a file that cannot be found.
A programming language used to write instructions a computer can follow.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.

coding-files-and-errors.question: Which response handles the missing score file clearly?
choices: Tell the player no saved score exists and start at 0
Claim the old score loaded successfully
coding-files-and-errors.feedback: A specific missing-file response explains what happened and provides a sensible starting value.
coding-files-and-errors.practice: Describe what your program should do if its reading-list file is missing. Explain how this differs from a file it cannot open because access is denied.

coding-modules-and-packages.title: Modules and Packages
explanation: A module is a unit of Python code, often saved in one file, that other code can use. A package organizes related modules under one name. A library is a collection of reusable code. Python includes a standard library: useful code supplied with Python. Importing a module makes its features available so you can use work that already exists.

Put related jobs together, such as score calculations in one module and screen messages in another. Read documentation, which explains how a feature is meant to work, before using it. Check what information a feature accepts and what it returns. The dot in math.sqrt names the sqrt feature inside math. Using a documented feature avoids rewriting it yourself, but you still need to choose inputs that fit its stated purpose.
coding-modules-and-packages.example: After import math, math.sqrt(81) returns 9.0. The math module supplies sqrt, a function that finds a nonnegative number whose square equals the given nonnegative number.

terms.definition: A unit of Python code that can be imported and used elsewhere.
A way to group related Python modules under one name.
Reusable code made available for programs to use.
Reusable code supplied with Python.
Make a module available to your Python code.
Written instructions describing how code should be used.
A named piece of code that can receive information and return a result.
A number which, multiplied by itself, gives the original number.
A programming language used to write instructions a computer can follow.
Information supplied to a program or model.
A capability or part of a program.

coding-modules-and-packages.question: In math.sqrt(81), what does math identify?
coding-modules-and-packages.feedback: math is the imported module, and sqrt identifies the feature you are calling inside it.
coding-modules-and-packages.practice: Find the documentation for math.ceil. Describe its job and predict its answer for 2.3 before checking.

coding-algorithms-and-complexity.title: Algorithms and Complexity
explanation: An algorithm is a clear sequence of steps for solving a problem. Two algorithms can find the same answer while doing different amounts of work. Complexity describes how that work grows as the input grows. Count a useful operation, such as comparing names, rather than assuming one particular computer speed. This helps you judge whether an approach will still work with a much bigger collection.

Linear search checks items one by one. Its worst case checks every item. Binary search works on sorted items: compare the middle item and discard the half that cannot contain the answer, then repeat. It needs the items in order and a way to reach the middle efficiently. Preparing that order also takes work. For a tiny or one-time search, the simpler approach may already be good enough.
coding-algorithms-and-complexity.example: With 16 sorted numbered cards, linear search may compare all 16. Binary search needs at most 5 comparisons to find a present card using the usual middle-item check.

terms.definition: A clear sequence of steps that solves a problem.
Information given to an algorithm.
How the work or storage needed changes as input grows.
Find an item by checking items one at a time.
Search ordered items by repeatedly keeping only the possible half.
Arranged in a stated order.
The input situation requiring the most work for that size.

coding-algorithms-and-complexity.question: Why can binary search discard half of the numbered cards?
choices: Because the cards are in order
Because every card has the same number
Because it has already read every card
coding-algorithms-and-complexity.feedback: Ordering tells you which side of the middle number could contain your target. Without that order, discarding half is unsafe.
coding-algorithms-and-complexity.practice: Use cards numbered 1 through 16 to search for 14 by checking the middle and keeping the possible half. Record each comparison.

sources.title: Python: binary search in sorted lists and performance
Cornell: algorithm complexity and input growth

coding-data-structures.title: Data Structures
explanation: A data structure is a way to arrange information so particular jobs are convenient. A stack adds and removes at the same end: the newest item is removed first. This fits an undo feature, which reverses the most recent action. A queue adds at one end and removes from the other: the oldest waiting item is handled first. This fits a line of print jobs.

Choose a structure by the operation you need most. A structure that makes adding easy may make finding an item in the middle slower. A Python deque, pronounced "deck," supports adding and removing at either end efficiently, so it can support a queue. A list, an ordered group of items, works well for reaching an item by its position. Explain the choice using the actual task, rather than saying one structure is always best.
coding-data-structures.example: Jobs arrive as A, then B, then C. A queue prints A first. If drawing actions arrive as A, B, C, an undo stack reverses C first.

terms.definition: An arrangement of information chosen to support useful operations.
A structure that removes the newest added item first.
A structure that removes the oldest waiting item first.
A job performed on stored information, such as adding or removing.
A Python collection designed for efficient adding and removing at both ends.
An ordered collection of items.
Gaining an advantage in one area while accepting a cost in another.
A programming language used to write instructions a computer can follow.
A capability or part of a program.

coding-data-structures.question: If A, B, and C arrive in that order, which should a queue handle first?
coding-data-structures.feedback: A has waited longest. A queue handles the oldest waiting item first.
coding-data-structures.practice: Choose stack or queue for reversing drawing actions and serving waiting players. Say which item would be handled first.

coding-testing-and-debugging.title: Testing and Debugging
explanation: A bug is a mistake that makes a program behave incorrectly. Debugging means finding and fixing its cause. Start by reproducing it: write down the input and steps that make the problem happen again. Then compare the expected result with the actual result. Look at a small part of the code and follow how its values change. Guessing at several changes at once makes the cause harder to identify.

A test is a check with a stated expected result. After finding the cause, make a focused correction and run the failing check again. Try nearby cases too, especially boundaries such as zero items or exactly the required score. Keep the check so later changes can reveal if the mistake returns. Passing tests provide evidence for the cases you checked; they do not prove every possible use is correct.
coding-testing-and-debugging.example: A ticket function charges twice the ticket count. A test expects 6 for 3 tickets but gets 5. You find an accidental subtraction and fix it; the test now gets 6.

terms.definition: A mistake that causes unwanted program behavior.
Finding and correcting the cause of a bug.
Repeat the steps that make a problem happen.
A check comparing actual behavior with an expected result.
An input at the edge of a condition or allowed range.
A named group of reusable instructions.
A saved check intended to catch a previously fixed mistake if it returns.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.
Information supplied to a program or model.

coding-testing-and-debugging.question: What is the most useful first check after fixing the ticket calculation?
choices: Run the 3-ticket test that exposed the mistake
coding-testing-and-debugging.feedback: The original failing case checks whether your correction addresses the observed problem. Nearby cases then add useful evidence.
coding-testing-and-debugging.practice: Write expected ticket costs for 0, 1, and 3 tickets at 2 coins each. Explain how these checks help.

coding-object-oriented-design.title: Object-Oriented Design
explanation: An object brings related information and actions together in a program. A class describes a kind of object; an instance is one particular object made from that class. A Pet class could describe a pet name and hunger amount. Two pet instances can hold different names and hunger amounts while using the same kind of instructions.

An attribute is information attached to an object, such as its name. A method is a function attached to that kind of object, such as feed(), which changes its hunger amount. Choose information and actions that belong together. Feeding one pet should change that pet, rather than every pet by accident. Objects help organize some programs, but a small calculation may only need a function. Start with the simplest organization that makes each job clear.
coding-object-oriented-design.example: Milo has hunger 5 and Luna has hunger 8. Calling Milo's feed method lowers Milo's hunger to 3. Luna's hunger stays 8 because it belongs to another instance.

terms.definition: A program value combining related information and behavior.
A description used to create a kind of object.
One particular object created from a class.
Information attached to an object.
A function associated with an object or class.
A named group of reusable instructions.
Organizing a program around objects with related data and actions.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.

coding-object-oriented-design.question: Which hunger amount should change when you feed only Milo?
coding-object-oriented-design.feedback: Each pet instance has its own hunger amount in this design. Milo's method changes Milo's information.
coding-object-oriented-design.practice: Describe a Book class with two attributes and one useful method. Make two instances with different values.

sources.title: Python: classes, instance variables, and methods

coding-recursion-and-invariants.title: Recursion and Invariants
explanation: Recursion means a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of its problem. A base case is a situation answered without another self-call. Each new call must move toward that case. Otherwise the calls keep growing until the program runs out of allowed space or time. To understand a recursive function, write down the calls first, then follow the answers as they return.

An invariant is a statement that stays true at a stated point in the steps. It helps explain why the process is correct. For a recursive sum, each call must still mean "the sum from 1 up to this nonnegative whole number." The number decreases, but the meaning of the job stays the same. Check the base case and the smaller step separately, and make clear which inputs your explanation allows.
coding-recursion-and-invariants.example: Define sum_to(0) as 0, and sum_to(n) as n + sum_to(n - 1) for positive whole numbers. sum_to(3) becomes 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6.

terms.definition: A named group of instructions that can return a result.
Solving a problem through a function calling itself on a smaller version.
A case answered without another recursive call.
A function call to that same function.
A statement that stays true at a chosen point in the steps.
Zero or greater.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.
Information supplied to a program or model.

coding-recursion-and-invariants.question: What makes sum_to stop making new calls for input 3?
choices: n decreases until the base case n = 0
coding-recursion-and-invariants.feedback: The calls use 3, 2, 1, and 0. The 0 case returns an answer directly, so no further self-call is needed.
coding-recursion-and-invariants.practice: Trace sum_to(2), showing both the calls and the returned answers. Explain why negative inputs need a different plan.

coding-concurrency-and-events.title: Concurrency and Events
explanation: Concurrency means more than one task can make progress during the same overall period. The tasks may take turns on one processor; they do not have to run at exactly the same instant. Parallelism means tasks actually run at the same time. An event is a notice that something happened, such as a button click or a finished download. An event handler is code that responds to that notice.

A browser can let a download wait for the network while still handling a click. Its event loop arranges when waiting work and responses get a turn. A long piece of code that does not give up its turn can delay other responses. Timing also matters when tasks share information: one task might read an old value before another updates it. Plan which result must be ready before the next job begins.
coding-concurrency-and-events.example: You start loading a picture, then click Cancel before it finishes. The cancel handler marks it canceled. When loading finishes, the response checks that mark before displaying the picture.

terms.definition: Multiple tasks making progress over the same period, possibly by taking turns.
Tasks running at the same instant.
The computer part that executes instructions.
A notice that an action or change occurred.
Code that responds to an event.
A mechanism that schedules work and event responses.
Connected computers through which information travels.

coding-concurrency-and-events.question: Why check the canceled mark when the picture finishes loading?
choices: Cancel may have happened while loading was waiting
coding-concurrency-and-events.feedback: The events can occur in that order. Checking the current canceled mark avoids displaying a picture the person already canceled.
coding-concurrency-and-events.practice: Put these events in two possible orders: loading starts, cancel is clicked, loading finishes. State what the screen should show in each.

sources.title: MDN: JavaScript execution model and event loop

coding-databases-and-persistence.title: Databases and Persistence
explanation: Persistence means keeping information after the program stops. A database is an organized store of information that a program can search and change. In a relational database, a table arranges information in rows and columns. A row describes one item, such as one book. A column describes a kind of information, such as its title or whether you have read it.

A query is a request for information from a database. SQL is a language for writing these requests. SELECT chooses what to return, FROM names the table, and WHERE gives a condition for choosing rows. Write the question in ordinary words before writing a query. Saving a change and getting it back are separate jobs, so check both. A database stored only in temporary computer memory will not automatically keep information after closing.
coding-databases-and-persistence.example: A books table has title and read columns. SELECT title FROM books WHERE read = 0 requests the titles of rows marked unread, if 0 is your unread marker.

terms.definition: Keeping information so it remains available after a program stops.
An organized store of information that can be searched and changed.
A database organizing information into related tables.
Data arranged in rows and columns.
One entry in a table.
One kind of information recorded for each entry.
A request for information from a database.
A language used to request and change information in relational databases.
SQL words for choosing returned information, naming its table, and filtering rows.
Temporary working storage used by a running computer.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.

coding-databases-and-persistence.question: If 0 means unread, what does the example query return?
coding-databases-and-persistence.feedback: WHERE read = 0 chooses unread rows, and SELECT title returns their titles.
coding-databases-and-persistence.practice: Draw a three-row books table. Mark one book read and two unread. Write the two titles that the example query should return.

coding-architecture-and-interfaces.title: Architecture and Interfaces
explanation: Software architecture is the plan for how a program's parts fit together. Give each part a clear responsibility, meaning the job it owns. In a study app, one part might show questions, another check answers, and another save scores. These parts still cooperate, but you can understand one job without reading every instruction in the whole program.

An interface states how parts communicate: what a part accepts, what it provides, and what problems it may report. For example, check_answer can accept a chosen answer and a correct answer, then return true or false. The screen part can use that result without knowing every checking step. Clear interfaces help you replace one part without rewriting every other part. Keep the agreement small and precise; confusing names or surprise behavior make cooperation harder.
coding-architecture-and-interfaces.example: The screen sends choice 2 and correct answer 2 to the checker. The checker returns true. The screen displays "Correct," and the score-saving part records the result.

terms.definition: The plan for a program's parts and how they cooperate.
The particular job assigned to a program part.
An agreement about information and results exchanged between parts.
Send a result back to the code that asked for it.
The two values representing whether a check is satisfied.
Giving different jobs to distinct program parts so each is easier to understand.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.

coding-architecture-and-interfaces.question: Which part should decide whether choice 2 matches correct answer 2?
coding-architecture-and-interfaces.feedback: The checker owns the matching decision. The other parts can use its result for their own jobs.
coding-architecture-and-interfaces.practice: Split a reading-list app into three parts. Write the information passed between two of them and the result expected back.

sources.title: Cornell: separating concerns and public interfaces

ai-ai-systems-and-tasks.title: AI Systems and Tasks
explanation: Artificial intelligence, or AI, means computer systems built to perform tasks such as finding solutions, recognizing patterns, or generating text. Some systems use instructions written by people; others learn patterns from examples. To describe a useful task, name its input, its output, and its goal. Input is what the system receives. Output is what it produces. The goal explains how that result should help someone.

Keep the task specific enough to check. "Be clever" gives you little to measure, but "identify which photos contain a bicycle" does. Think about mistakes too: a system might miss a bicycle or identify one where there is none. Decide who will check uncertain results and whether the available information is enough for the task. A system can perform one task well without being good at every other task.
ai-ai-systems-and-tasks.example: A photo sorter receives a photo as input and outputs "bicycle" or "no bicycle." Its goal is to help organize a collection by identifying photos containing bicycles.

terms.definition: Computer systems built to perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, finding solutions, or generating content.
Software and other parts working together to carry out an AI task.
Information given to a system.
Information or actions produced by a system.
The useful result you want the system to achieve.
A repeated relationship in information.

ai-ai-systems-and-tasks.question: What is the output of the bicycle photo sorter?
ai-ai-systems-and-tasks.feedback: The photo is the input. The system produces a category result, and that result helps organize photos.
ai-ai-systems-and-tasks.practice: Describe a system that helps find songs you like. Name one input, one output, and a goal that you could check.

sources.title: Poole and Mackworth: designing AI tasks

ai-search-and-state-spaces.title: Search and State Spaces
explanation: AI search explores possible steps to find a solution. A state describes the situation at one point. An action is a move that can change it. A state space is the collection of situations the problem allows. A goal test checks whether a state solves the problem. For a maze, a state can be your current square, an action can be a legal move, and the goal test can ask whether you reached the exit.

Start by describing the allowed moves clearly. A wall blocks a move, and a move cannot leave the maze. Search may need to try several paths and remember places already visited so it does not keep repeating the same route. Finding any route and finding the shortest route are different goals. The best search approach depends on which goal you chose and how much information the state records.
ai-search-and-state-spaces.example: In a three-square hallway, start at A, move right to B, then right to exit C. The goal test is false at A and B, and true at C.

terms.definition: Exploring possible steps to find a solution.
A description of the situation at one point.
An allowed step that can change a state.
The collection of states possible in a problem.
A check asking whether the current state meets the goal.
A sequence of states or moves from a starting point.
Computer systems built for tasks such as recognizing patterns, finding solutions, or generating content.

ai-search-and-state-spaces.question: What does the goal test ask in the hallway example?
ai-search-and-state-spaces.feedback: The stated goal is to reach exit C, so the goal test checks whether the current square is C.
ai-search-and-state-spaces.practice: Draw a small maze with a start and exit. Name its states and actions, then give a goal test in one sentence.

ai-data-and-features.title: Data and Features
explanation: Data is recorded information. In a learning task, an example is one case the system studies. A feature is an input detail used to make a prediction, such as a fruit's weight or color. A label is the known answer for an example, such as "apple." A dataset is a collection of examples. Learning from examples with known answers is called supervised learning.

Keep features and labels distinct. If the job is to predict the fruit name, that name is the answer you want, so it should not secretly be part of the input. Choose details that will actually be available when a new fruit arrives. Check whether examples cover the fruits and conditions you expect. A collection containing only red apples cannot teach a system everything about green apples, bananas, or unfamiliar fruits.
ai-data-and-features.example: One recorded fruit weighs 150 grams and is green; its label is "apple." Weight and color are features. "Apple" is the answer the model is learning to predict.

terms.definition: Recorded information.
One case used for learning or checking.
An input detail used to make a prediction.
The known answer attached to an example.
A collection of examples.
An answer estimated for a case.
Learning patterns from examples with known answers.
The learned mathematical pattern used to make predictions.
Information supplied to a program or model.

ai-data-and-features.question: When predicting a fruit name, which is the label in the example?
ai-data-and-features.feedback: Apple is the known fruit name, which is the answer being predicted. Weight and color are input features.
ai-data-and-features.practice: Make three pretend fruit records. Identify each record's features and label. Say which detail you must avoid giving away as an input.

sources.title: Google: supervised learning features and labels

ai-rules-and-logic.title: Rules and Logic
explanation: Logic studies which conclusions follow from stated information. A fact is a statement you accept as true for the problem. A rule connects statements, such as "If a creature is a bird, it is an animal." Inference means using facts and rules to reach a supported conclusion. A computer can follow these connections step by step without learning from a pile of examples.

For this method, the conclusion depends on the facts and rules you supplied. If one is wrong, the resulting conclusion may also be wrong about the world. Follow the direction of a rule carefully. "Every bird is an animal" does not mean every animal is a bird. Also, having no statement about a creature does not automatically prove the opposite statement. Say what follows, what does not follow, and which information is still missing.
ai-rules-and-logic.example: Fact: Pip is a bird. Rule: if something is a bird, it is an animal. Supported conclusion: Pip is an animal. The rule alone says nothing about whether Pip can fly.

terms.definition: Reasoning about which conclusions follow from stated information.
A statement accepted as true within a problem.
A stated connection saying what follows when its conditions hold.
Deriving a conclusion from facts and rules.
A statement reached through reasoning.
A statement connecting a condition to what follows when it holds.

ai-rules-and-logic.question: Which conclusion follows from the Pip example?
ai-rules-and-logic.feedback: The fact matches the rule's condition, so the rule supports Pip being an animal. It does not establish flying.
ai-rules-and-logic.practice: Use the fact "This shape is a square" and the rule "Every square has four sides." State a supported conclusion and one thing these statements do not tell you.

sources.title: Poole and Mackworth: definite clauses and inference

ai-classification-and-regression.title: Classification and Regression
explanation: Classification predicts a category. A category is a named group, such as "apple" or "banana." Regression predicts a number, such as how much a fruit weighs. Both can use a model, a learned mathematical pattern connecting input details to answers. Choose the kind of prediction by asking what you want the answer to mean.

Numbers can sometimes be category names. A jersey number used to identify a player is different from a predicted height you can measure. Ask whether the task is choosing among groups or estimating an amount. Also ask how you will judge a mistake. A wrong fruit category can be counted as incorrect; a weight estimate can be compared with the measured weight to see how far off it is. Clear goals make the result easier to check.
ai-classification-and-regression.example: A fruit program predicts "apple" for one task and 150 grams for another. The fruit-name task is classification. Estimating weight is regression, even if the estimate happens to be a whole number.

terms.definition: Predicting which category an example belongs to.
A named group used as an answer.
Predicting a numerical amount.
A learned mathematical pattern used to make predictions.
An estimated answer for an input.
Information supplied to a model.
A set of instructions a computer can follow.
The known answer attached to a learning example.

ai-classification-and-regression.question: Which task is regression?
choices: Estimating a fruit's weight in grams
ai-classification-and-regression.feedback: Weight is a numerical amount. Apple/banana and ripe/unripe are categories.
ai-classification-and-regression.practice: Label these tasks classification or regression: predict a bus arrival time, identify an animal, estimate a book's page count. Explain your choices.

ai-training-and-evaluation.title: Training and Evaluation
explanation: Training is the process of changing a model using examples so it can make useful predictions. A model is a learned mathematical pattern. Evaluation means checking how well its predictions work. To get a useful check, use examples that were kept apart from the training work. Otherwise you may only discover that the model remembers examples it has already seen.

A training set supplies practice examples. A validation set helps you choose or adjust your approach. A test set checks the finished choice. Repeatedly changing your approach after seeing test results makes that test less independent. Overfitting means fitting the training examples so closely that predictions on new examples work poorly. Keep related copies together when splitting data, and make sure your checking examples resemble the real situations you care about.
ai-training-and-evaluation.example: A digit reader learns from one group of handwriting pictures. You check it on different pictures it did not learn from. New handwriting gives better evidence than repeating the exact practice pictures.

terms.definition: Using examples to adjust a model.
A learned mathematical pattern used to make predictions.
Checking how well a system performs its task.
Examples used to learn the model.
Separate examples used to choose or adjust an approach.
Separate examples used to check a finished choice.

ai-training-and-evaluation.question: Which pictures make the most useful independent check of the digit reader?
choices: Only exact pictures used for practice
Different handwriting pictures kept out of training
Pictures with the correct digit written into the input
ai-training-and-evaluation.feedback: Held-apart examples check whether learning works on new cases. Repeated practice pictures can hide overfitting.
ai-training-and-evaluation.practice: Divide nine pretend examples into training, validation, and test groups. Explain which group you would use to choose between two model designs.

ai-decision-trees-and-neighbors.title: Decision Trees and Neighbors
explanation: A decision tree predicts by following a series of questions. Each branch is a possible answer, and a leaf is an ending that gives a prediction. A fruit tree might ask "Is it heavier than 100 grams?" and then "Is it yellow?" Following the answers takes you to a fruit category. A learned tree chooses these questions from examples rather than relying only on questions written by a person.

A nearest-neighbor method compares a new example with stored examples. It chooses the closest ones according to a stated distance measure, meaning a way to score how different their features are. For three-neighbor classification, three close examples vote on a category. The comparison needs sensible features and units: measuring weight in grams versus kilograms can change the result if you do not account for the scale.
ai-decision-trees-and-neighbors.example: For a new fruit, the three closest stored examples are labeled apple, apple, and pear. A three-neighbor majority vote predicts apple because two of the three labels are apple.

An ending of a decision tree that supplies a prediction.

ai-decision-trees-and-neighbors.question: What does the three-neighbor vote predict from apple, apple, pear?
ai-decision-trees-and-neighbors.feedback: Two of the three closest examples are apples, so apple wins the majority vote.
ai-decision-trees-and-neighbors.practice: Draw a two-question fruit tree. Then invent three nearby labeled examples and show a majority vote for a new fruit.

ai-probability-and-uncertainty.title: Probability and Uncertainty
explanation: Probability describes how likely an outcome is, using numbers from 0 to 1 or percentages from 0% to 100%. A probabilistic model gives estimated chances instead of claiming every answer is certain. It might assign an 80% chance to "apple" and a 20% chance to "pear." These are estimates based on what the model learned, and they can be mistaken.

Calibration asks whether predicted chances match how often outcomes occur. If a model is well calibrated, then among many similar cases assigned about 80% chance of apple, roughly 80% should actually be apples. That does not guarantee the answer for one fruit. A model can sound certain and still be unreliable when inputs are unfamiliar or its estimates are poorly calibrated. Check the estimates against real results before relying on their numbers.
ai-probability-and-uncertainty.example: Out of 100 fruits each assigned about an 80% apple chance, a well-calibrated model would have about 80 actual apples. The remaining fruits show why 80% is not certainty.

terms.definition: A number expressing how likely an outcome is.

ai-probability-and-uncertainty.question: What does an 80% apple estimate mean for one new fruit?
choices: It is an estimated chance, and the fruit can still be something else
It proves the fruit is an apple
Exactly 80% of that fruit is apple
ai-probability-and-uncertainty.feedback: The number expresses an estimated likelihood, not a guarantee or a fraction of the fruit itself.
ai-probability-and-uncertainty.practice: Invent ten predictions near 70% for an outcome. About how many successes would support good calibration? Explain why ten cases provide limited evidence.

ai-neural-network-basics.title: Neural Network Basics
explanation: A neural network is a model made from connected calculations arranged in layers. A model is a mathematical system used to predict or produce results. Input layers receive numbers, hidden layers perform intermediate calculations, and an output layer produces a result. A node is one calculation point. A weight is an adjustable number that multiplies an incoming value, changing its contribution.

A node often adds weighted inputs and a bias, an adjustable extra number. It then applies an activation function, a calculation that changes this sum. For example, one activation keeps positive numbers and changes negative numbers to zero. These changes let networks represent more than simple straight-line relationships. During training, learning adjusts weights and biases to reduce prediction errors. Extra layers alone do not guarantee better answers; the calculations, examples, and checking all matter.
ai-neural-network-basics.example: One node receives 2, multiplies by weight 3, adds bias 1, and keeps positive results: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. Changing its weight to 4 gives 9.

ai-neural-network-basics.question: What does the example node output when its weight changes from 3 to 4?
ai-neural-network-basics.feedback: The new calculation is 2 × 4 + 1 = 9, and the activation keeps that positive number.
ai-neural-network-basics.practice: Change the bias to 0 while keeping input 2 and weight 4. Work out the result and identify which quantity you changed.

sources.title: Google: neural network nodes and hidden layers

ai-language-models.title: Language Models
explanation: A language model learns patterns in text and estimates which pieces of text fit a context. A token is a piece of text used by the model: it may be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation. Context is the information available for the current answer, including the request and earlier text that fits within the model's allowed space.

To generate text, many current language models predict possible next tokens, choose one, add it to the context, and repeat. Different choices can produce different answers to the same request. The patterns can support useful explanations and writing, but a likely continuation is not the same as a verified fact. A model may produce a smooth sentence with an incorrect date or invented reference. Check factual details against dependable sources when correctness matters.
ai-language-models.example: After "The cat sat on the," a model might continue with "mat." Changing the context to "The cat climbed the" changes which next tokens are likely. Neither completion proves a real cat did anything.

terms.definition: A model that estimates patterns and probabilities in sequences of text.

The information available to a model when it produces its next result.

choices: The model watched this exact cat
Every sentence must end in mat
It fits text patterns and the available context
ai-language-models.feedback: The model uses learned text patterns and context. A plausible completion does not establish an event in the real world.
ai-language-models.practice: Write two sentence beginnings using the word bank for different meanings. Suggest a likely continuation for each and explain how context changes it.

sources.title: Google: large language models and limitations

ai-reinforcement-learning.title: Reinforcement Learning
explanation: Reinforcement learning is a way to learn actions from feedback over time. An agent is the part that chooses actions. The environment is the situation it acts in. An action changes that situation, and a reward is a number used as feedback. A policy is the agent's method for choosing its next action. Learning aims for more reward across a sequence of actions.

For a maze game, the agent can move between squares, and reaching the exit can earn points. An action with little reward now may be useful if it helps reach a bigger reward later. Exploration means trying actions to find out what happens; exploitation means choosing actions that already seem useful. Design rewards carefully, because a system can learn to collect points in ways that fail to match your intended goal.
ai-reinforcement-learning.example: In a pretend maze, the agent is a moving marker, the actions are up/down/left/right, the environment is the maze, and the reward is 10 points for reaching the exit.

terms.definition: Learning to choose actions using rewards from interaction over time.

The situation the agent acts within.

A number used as feedback about what happened.
A method for choosing actions.
Trying actions to learn their effects.
Choosing actions already expected to work well.

ai-reinforcement-learning.question: What is the reward in the pretend maze setup?
choices: The 10 points for reaching the exit
ai-reinforcement-learning.feedback: The marker is the agent and the directions are actions. The points provide reward feedback.
ai-reinforcement-learning.practice: Design rewards for a pretend cleanup game. Explain how a badly chosen reward could encourage moving mess around instead of removing it.

sources.title: OpenAI Spinning Up: reinforcement learning concepts

ai-generative-ai.title: Generative AI
explanation: Generative AI produces content such as text, pictures, sound, or video using patterns learned from data. Data is information used for learning. A prompt is the request or material you give the system. The output is the content it produces. Some tasks invite invented content, such as a dragon story. Other tasks need accurate content, such as a description of an actual animal.

Compare outputs against the job you requested. Does each follow the instructions? Does it include every required detail? If it makes claims about the real world, can you verify them? A realistic picture can show something that never happened, and fluent text can contain invented facts. One impressive example does not show that every output is reliable. State the limitation you noticed and decide whether to revise, verify, or reject the output.
ai-generative-ai.example: A school notice says "Trip: Friday at 10 a.m." You ask AI to summarize it. Output A repeats that time. Output B says "Saturday at 8 a.m." B contradicts the supplied notice.

terms.definition: AI that produces content from patterns learned in data.
Recorded information used for learning.
A request or supplied material given to a generative system.

Check a claim against dependable evidence.

ai-generative-ai.question: Which step best helps compare the two notice summaries?
choices: Compare each summary with the original notice
Assume both are true because they were generated
ai-generative-ai.feedback: The notice provides the stated day and time. Comparing with it reveals that output B changed the facts.
ai-generative-ai.practice: Write a prompt for a made-up animal story and one for facts about a real animal. Explain how you would judge the outputs differently.

ai-model-robustness.title: Model Robustness
explanation: Robustness means a system continues to work acceptably when it meets changes relevant to its job. A model is a learned mathematical pattern used to make predictions. A model trained on bright, clear pictures may struggle with dark or blurry ones. Test ordinary changes you expect rather than assuming success on familiar examples carries over to every situation.

Data shift means the information a system meets in use differs from the information it learned or was checked on. The change might involve a new camera, a different background, or a different mix of objects. Measure performance on those changed cases. If it drops, you may need better examples, a different approach, or a clear limit on where the system is used. Robustness is always about specified changes; no small test proves a system handles all possible changes.
ai-model-robustness.example: A bicycle detector recognizes 18 of 20 clear test photos, but only 9 of 20 dark photos. The lighting change reveals a weakness that the clear-photo score did not show.

terms.definition: Maintaining acceptable performance under specified changes.
A learned mathematical pattern used for prediction.
Using examples to adjust a model.
A difference between data used to learn or check a system and data met in use.
How well a system carries out its task.
A system that identifies whether a specified thing is present.

ai-model-robustness.question: What does the drop from 18 to 9 recognized bicycles reveal?
choices: The dark photos are guaranteed to contain no bicycles
The system handles every lighting condition
The system has trouble under the tested lighting change
ai-model-robustness.feedback: Performance drops on dark photos, so bright-photo success does not establish robustness to this lighting change.
ai-model-robustness.practice: Propose three ordinary changes to test for a handwriting reader. State one result that would reveal a weakness.

sources.title: Google: monitoring data and model performance

ai-fairness-and-bias.title: Fairness and Bias
explanation: Bias in an AI system can mean a repeated skew in its information or results that disadvantages people. It can start with which examples were collected, how answers were labeled, or how the system is used. A speech reader trained mostly on one accent may make more mistakes for speakers with another accent. The people receiving more mistakes experience the practical effect.

Fairness asks how people should be treated in the particular task. There are different ways to measure fair treatment, and one score does not settle every question. Compare error patterns across relevant groups and ask affected people what the mistakes mean for them. More varied examples may help, but they do not guarantee fair outcomes. Check the updated system again and consider whether the task or the way results are used also needs to change.
ai-fairness-and-bias.example: A voice study app understands 19 of 20 requests from one tested accent group and 12 of 20 from another. The second group faces more failed requests even if the overall score looks useful.

terms.definition: A repeated skew in information or results that can disadvantage people.
Considering how people should be treated in a particular task.
Using examples to adjust a system.
An answer attached to a learning example.
The fraction of checked cases with mistakes.
A way of pronouncing words associated with a person or group.
Computer systems built for tasks such as recognizing patterns, finding solutions, or generating content.

ai-fairness-and-bias.question: Who receives more failed requests in the voice-app example?
choices: The group with 12 of 20 understood requests
Both groups receive exactly the same number
The group with 19 of 20 understood requests
ai-fairness-and-bias.feedback: The first group has 1 failed request, and the second has 8. Comparing groups exposes a difference that one overall score can hide.
ai-fairness-and-bias.practice: Invent a picture-sorting task. Name one group or condition missing from its training examples and explain who could receive more errors.

ai-privacy-and-safety.title: Privacy and Safety
explanation: Privacy concerns what personal information is collected, who can access it, and how it is used. Personal information can include names, addresses, photos, and private messages. Safety concerns preventing harm from a system's behavior. Before using an AI feature, ask which information the task really needs and what could happen if the output is wrong or the information reaches someone unintended.

A safeguard is a step that reduces a specific risk. For a practice writing tool, use a made-up name instead of a real name if identity is unnecessary. Limit access to saved writing and provide a way to remove it. For a task where a wrong answer could hurt someone, make sure a qualified person checks the result before it guides action. Choose safeguards that fit the task, then check whether they work.
ai-privacy-and-safety.example: A story helper asks for a child's home address even though it only needs a made-up character and setting. Remove the address request; it adds private information without helping this task.

terms.definition: Decisions and protections concerning personal information and its use.
Information that identifies or concerns a person.
Preventing or reducing harm from a system.
The possibility of harm in a particular situation.
A step intended to reduce a stated risk.
The ability or permission to view or use information.
Collecting only the information needed for the stated purpose.
Computer systems built for tasks such as recognizing patterns, finding solutions, or generating content.

ai-privacy-and-safety.feedback: The task can work without a home address. Avoiding that collection reduces the specific privacy risk.
ai-privacy-and-safety.practice: Imagine a study app saving voice recordings. Name one privacy concern and one safeguard directly addressing it.

ai-ai-system-evaluation.title: AI System Evaluation
explanation: AI system evaluation checks whether a whole system works for its intended use. Accuracy is the fraction of checked predictions that are correct, but that number alone can hide important mistakes. A false positive says something is present when it is absent. A false negative misses something that is present. Which mistake matters more depends on the job and the people affected.

Choose test cases that match likely use, including difficult cases and different user groups. Compare the system with a simple alternative, such as a person checking a list. Record useful results, missed cases, wrong alerts, response time, and effects on people. Set a success condition before checking, and explain the limits of the evidence. After the system is used, keep checking because inputs and behavior can change.
ai-ai-system-evaluation.example: A homework reminder correctly handles 18 of 20 tasks, but its two mistakes are missed deadlines. Its 90% accuracy hides a serious weakness if the main goal is preventing missed deadlines.

terms.definition: Checking performance, limitations, and effects for an intended use.
The fraction of checked predictions that are correct.
An alert or positive answer when the specified thing is absent.
A missed alert or negative answer when the specified thing is present.
One situation used to check a system.
A simple alternative used for comparison.
A stated requirement used to judge whether a task worked.
Computer systems built for tasks such as recognizing patterns, finding solutions, or generating content.
Information supplied to a program or model.

choices: Only the color of the alert
Only whether the number looks large
The missed deadlines and their effect on users
ai-ai-system-evaluation.feedback: The two mistakes concern the main goal. Their type and practical effect matter, even when most other cases are correct.
ai-ai-system-evaluation.practice: Design a check for a library-book reminder. Name two kinds of mistake, one simple comparison, and a success condition.

quantum-complex-numbers.title: Complex Numbers
explanation: A complex number has two parts. In 3 + 4i, the real part is 3 and the imaginary part is 4. The symbol i is a number defined by i × i = −1. “Imaginary” is the mathematical name; it does not mean the number is useless or pretend. Draw the number as a point: three steps right and four steps up.

An arrow from zero to that point has a length and a direction. Its length is the magnitude. Its angle from the rightward line is the phase. Quantum physics uses complex numbers as probability amplitudes. Squaring an amplitude’s magnitude gives an outcome’s probability when the whole state is properly scaled. Phase helps determine how amplitudes combine.
quantum-complex-numbers.example: For 3 + 4i, the magnitude is 5: 3² + 4² = 25, and 5² = 25. The number 5 has the same magnitude but a different phase.

terms.definition: A number with a real part and an imaginary part.
The number whose square is −1.

The angle of a complex number’s arrow.
A complex number used to calculate a quantum measurement probability.
A number from 0 to 1 describing the chance of an outcome.
The physics used to describe systems such as atoms and electrons.
The ordinary-number part of a complex number, such as 3 in 3 + 4i.
The ordinary number multiplying i, such as 4 in 3 + 4i.

quantum-complex-numbers.question: What differs between 3 + 4i and 5?
choices: Their phase, while their magnitude matches
quantum-complex-numbers.feedback: Both arrows have length 5. One points diagonally, and the other points right.
quantum-complex-numbers.practice: Draw arrows for 1, i, −1, and −i. Compare their lengths and directions.

quantum-probability-and-waves.title: Probability and Waves
explanation: Quantum physics predicts the chances of measurement results using numbers called amplitudes. Amplitudes can combine in a wave-like way. Depending on their phase, they can strengthen or cancel each other. This is interference. We combine the relevant amplitudes first, then square the magnitude of the result to find a probability. Adding the probabilities first can give the wrong answer.

In a two-slit experiment, electrons reach a screen as separate detected spots. When both openings are available and the setup does not reveal which opening each electron used, many detections can build a striped pattern. The wave-like calculation predicts where spots are more or less likely. It does not supply a little drawn route for each electron.
quantum-probability-and-waves.example: At one screen location, two equal amplitudes with opposite phases cancel. That location can have a very small detection chance even though either opening alone could contribute there.
quantum-probability-and-waves.analogy: Water ripples can strengthen or cancel when they meet. The comparison helps with interference; a quantum amplitude is not water, and a detected electron is not a water ripple.

terms.definition: A number used to calculate the chance of a quantum outcome.
A quantity describing how an amplitude combines with other amplitudes.
Amplitudes combining to strengthen or weaken a possible outcome.
A tiny negatively charged particle found in atoms.
A narrow opening.
The chance of an outcome, from 0 to 1.
The size of a number, ignoring its direction or phase.
An experiment using two narrow openings and a screen to study detection patterns.

quantum-probability-and-waves.question: Why can a location become dark when both openings are available?
quantum-probability-and-waves.feedback: Opposite amplitudes can cancel. The final probability is never negative.
quantum-probability-and-waves.practice: Draw two equal arrows pointing opposite ways. Add them head to tail and explain why their total length is zero.

quantum-superposition.title: Superposition
explanation: A quantum state is a mathematical description used to predict a system’s measurements. A superposition combines states with amplitudes. For a qubit, the usual measurement has two possible answers: 0 and 1. A state can contain contributions from both. The contributions include phase information, which affects what happens when we apply operations before measuring.

This is more than having a definite answer hidden from us. Two superpositions can give the same 0-or-1 chances but respond differently to a later operation because their relative phases differ. Also, “superposition” depends on the states we choose for comparison. A combination in one measurement arrangement can be a definite state in another. One measurement still records one result.
quantum-superposition.example: A qubit in the plus state gives 0 or 1 with equal chance in the usual measurement. Applying a Hadamard gate first makes the ideal result definitely 0.

terms.definition: A mathematical description that predicts measurement results.
A combination of reference states with probability amplitudes.
A number that contributes to a quantum state and its outcome chances.
A quantum system with two reference states, usually called 0 and 1.
The phase difference between two amplitudes.
A controlled operation that changes a quantum state.
An operation that converts 0 to the plus state and converts the plus state back to 0.
An equal superposition of 0 and 1 with matching phases.
A quantity describing how an amplitude combines with others.
A description combining states with ordinary probabilities, rather than combining their amplitudes.

quantum-superposition.question: What does a Hadamard gate do to the ideal plus state before the usual measurement?
choices: It returns both digits in one measurement
quantum-superposition.feedback: The gate combines the amplitudes so the 1 contribution cancels and the 0 outcome becomes certain.
quantum-superposition.practice: Explain why equal 0-or-1 chances alone do not tell you whether a state is a superposition or an ordinary random mixture.

quantum-measurement-outcomes.title: Measurement Outcomes
explanation: A quantum calculation can predict a distribution of outcomes: the chance of each answer when a measurement is made. That prediction differs from the answer in one run. If the chance of 1 is 25%, one run still gives either 0 or 1. It does not give one-quarter of a 1, and it does not promise a 1 on every fourth run.

To check the prediction, prepare the same state again, use the same measurement, and repeat many times. The share of results equal to 1 should usually approach 25% as the number of trials grows. Short runs can differ by chance. Measuring can also change the state, so repeatedly measuring one system is not always the same as preparing many identical trials.
quantum-measurement-outcomes.example: In 100 fresh trials, a prediction of 25% for 1 suggests roughly 25 results of 1. Getting 23 does not automatically mean the prediction failed.

terms.definition: A physical process that produces a recorded result about a system.
The list of possible outcomes and their probabilities.
The chance of an outcome, from 0 to 1.
A mathematical description used to predict a quantum system’s results.
One run of an experiment under stated conditions.

quantum-measurement-outcomes.question: If the prediction is 25% for 1, must 100 trials give exactly 25 ones?
choices: No, the count can vary by chance
quantum-measurement-outcomes.feedback: A probability predicts the pattern across repeated trials. It does not fix the exact count in a short run.
quantum-measurement-outcomes.practice: Write a possible list of 12 results with three ones. Write another plausible list with four ones.

sources.title: IBM Quantum: Build and run your first quantum program

quantum-wavefunctions-and-probability.title: Wavefunctions and Probability
explanation: A wavefunction assigns an amplitude to each position in a quantum model. The amplitude itself is not the chance of finding the particle there. Its magnitude squared gives the probability density. To find the chance of detecting the particle within a region, add up that density across the region. On a graph, this means finding the area under the density curve.

A normalized wavefunction has total probability 1 across all possible positions. That is 100%: the particle must be found somewhere allowed by the model if a position result is obtained. A high density makes a small region more likely than an equally wide region with lower density. The curve describes detection chances; it is not an outline of the particle or a track it follows.
quantum-wavefunctions-and-probability.example: Suppose the area under a normalized density curve is 0.30 in the left region and 0.70 in the right. The predicted detection chances are 30% left and 70% right.

terms.definition: A mathematical function assigning amplitudes to possible positions or other outcomes.
A number used to calculate a quantum outcome’s chance.
A number’s magnitude multiplied by itself.
A quantity whose area over a region gives the detection probability there.
Scaled so all possible outcome probabilities add up to 1.
A physical entity such as an electron.
A mathematical description that predicts results for a quantum system.

quantum-wavefunctions-and-probability.question: What is the predicted chance of detecting the particle in the right region?
quantum-wavefunctions-and-probability.feedback: The probability comes from the area over that region: 0.70 means 70%.
quantum-wavefunctions-and-probability.practice: Draw two rectangles whose areas are 0.30 and 0.70. Label their sum as total probability 1.

quantum-uncertainty-relations.title: Uncertainty Relations
explanation: An uncertainty relation describes limits on the spreads of certain measurement results for a prepared quantum state. Position and momentum are one such pair. Position tells us where something is. Momentum describes its amount and direction of motion. Prepare many copies of a state and measure position on some and momentum on others. Each set of results has a spread.

The product of those two spreads cannot be smaller than a fixed quantum limit. Making the position spread extremely narrow therefore requires a larger momentum spread. This is a property of the state, even with ideal measuring tools. It is not simply a clumsy observer bumping the particle. It also does not say that every pair of measurable quantities has the same limit.
quantum-uncertainty-relations.example: If an electron’s position results are tightly grouped in a narrow region, its momentum results cannot also be arbitrarily tightly grouped. Better instruments do not remove that relation.

terms.definition: A mathematical limit linking the spreads of paired measurement results.
How widely results differ from their average.
Where something is.
Mass multiplied by velocity in ordinary physics; a measurable motion quantity in quantum physics.
A mathematical description of a prepared quantum system.
A tiny negatively charged particle.
Speed together with direction.

quantum-uncertainty-relations.question: Why can perfect instruments not make both spreads arbitrarily small?
choices: All measurements have the same answer
The state itself obeys an uncertainty relation
quantum-uncertainty-relations.feedback: The limit concerns the possible quantum state, not only the quality of the equipment.
quantum-uncertainty-relations.practice: Draw one narrow position-result cluster and one wide momentum-result cluster. Explain what the widths mean.

quantum-schrodinger-equation.title: Schrodinger Equation
explanation: The Schrödinger equation tells us how a quantum state changes with time in a standard quantum model. It uses the system’s energy description and its starting wavefunction. Energy includes motion energy and energy associated with position or interactions. Solving the equation gives a wavefunction for later times. From that, we calculate the chances of measurement results.

A related form of the equation finds states with definite energy when the energy description does not change with time. The surroundings and the conditions at the edges help decide which solutions are allowed. The equation predicts states and probabilities, rather than drawing a tiny object’s exact route. You can understand its job before learning the harder mathematics used to solve it.
quantum-schrodinger-equation.example: For an electron confined to a model box, the equation and the box’s edge conditions allow certain energy states. Choosing a different box size changes those allowed energies.

terms.definition: An equation connecting a quantum state’s change with the system’s energy.
A mathematical description used to predict quantum measurements.
A function assigning probability amplitudes to possible outcomes.
A physical quantity transferred in processes such as motion, heating, and light emission.
A mathematical result that satisfies an equation.
A tiny negatively charged particle.
Requirements that a model’s solution must satisfy at its boundaries.
A number used to calculate an outcome’s probability.

quantum-schrodinger-equation.question: What does solving the equation for the box help us find?
choices: The electron’s exact little road map

quantum-schrodinger-equation.feedback: The equation and edge conditions determine which wavefunctions and energies fit the model.
quantum-schrodinger-equation.practice: Explain the input and output in one sentence: starting state plus energy description leads to what?

quantum-bound-states-and-tunneling.title: Bound States and Tunneling
explanation: A bound state describes a particle held in a region by its surroundings. In simple quantum models, only certain bound-state energies are allowed. This is called quantization. For an ideal box with impenetrable walls, only particular wavefunction patterns fit the edge conditions. Different allowed patterns correspond to different energies; the particle cannot have just any bound-state energy.

A finite barrier is different from an impenetrable wall. A particle can have some chance of being detected beyond a narrow barrier even when its energy is below the barrier’s height. This is tunneling. The wavefunction extends through the barrier, and its size usually falls within it. For the same simple barrier shape and incoming energy, making the barrier wider usually reduces the passing chance. Energy conservation still holds.
quantum-bound-states-and-tunneling.example: An electron meets a narrow energy barrier. Some identically prepared trials detect it beyond the barrier. Widening that barrier, while keeping the other conditions fixed, makes those detections less likely.

terms.definition: A state in which a particle is held in a limited region.
Having only particular allowed values, such as certain energies.
A function used to calculate quantum measurement probabilities.
A region with potential energy higher than nearby regions.
A quantum process allowing passage through a finite energy barrier.
A tiny negatively charged particle.
Total energy is preserved when all energy transfers are counted.
Requirements at the boundaries of a model.
Energy associated with position or interactions.

quantum-bound-states-and-tunneling.question: What usually happens when this simple barrier gets wider?
quantum-bound-states-and-tunneling.feedback: For these fixed conditions, the wavefunction decreases across more barrier width, reducing the passing chance.
quantum-bound-states-and-tunneling.practice: Sketch a narrow barrier and a wider one. Label which has the smaller passing chance under the same conditions.

quantum-spin-and-angular-momentum.title: Spin and Angular Momentum
explanation: Angular momentum is a physical quantity connected with rotation. In quantum physics, orbital angular momentum comes from a particle’s spatial state. It is not a promise that an electron travels around an atom on a little circular track. Spin is a different, built-in kind of angular momentum. An electron has spin even when there is no ordinary orbit to describe.

The name “spin” can mislead us: an electron is not modeled as a small solid ball rotating on an axle. When we measure its spin along a chosen direction, we get one of two allowed values, often called spin up and spin down. Those names describe measurement results relative to that direction. Changing the measurement direction changes which states count as up or down.
quantum-spin-and-angular-momentum.example: Two electrons can occupy the same spatial orbital if their spin states differ. The spatial description matches, but the complete single-electron states do not.

terms.definition: A measurable quantity associated with rotation or a quantum system’s spin.
Angular momentum associated with a particle’s spatial state.
A built-in quantum form of angular momentum.
A tiny negatively charged particle.
A spatial wavefunction for an electron in an atom.
The two electron-spin outcomes along a chosen measurement direction.
A mathematical description used to predict measurements.

quantum-spin-and-angular-momentum.question: How can two electrons share a spatial orbital in this example?
choices: They must be the same complete state
quantum-spin-and-angular-momentum.feedback: Different spin states make their complete single-electron states different.
quantum-spin-and-angular-momentum.practice: Write two columns: orbital angular momentum and spin. State where each comes from.

quantum-hydrogen-and-orbitals.title: Hydrogen and Orbitals
explanation: A hydrogen atom has one electron and, in its simplest form, one proton. Their electric attraction allows bound states with particular energies. An orbital is the electron’s spatial wavefunction, used to calculate where detection is likely. It is not a planet-style orbit. Drawings of orbitals often show regions containing a chosen large share of the detection probability, rather than a hard wall.

Quantum numbers label the allowed states. The number n labels the main energy level in the simplest hydrogen model. The number l labels orbital angular momentum and connects with the orbital’s shape type. The number m labels its component along a chosen direction. These labels work together: for n = 1, only l = 0 is allowed. That orbital is called 1s.
quantum-hydrogen-and-orbitals.example: The 1s orbital has a probability pattern that is the same in every direction from the center. A 2p orbital has a different pattern and belongs to n = 2.

terms.definition: The element whose atoms have one proton.
A tiny negatively charged particle.
A positively charged particle in an atom’s center.
A state held near a region by an interaction.
An electron’s spatial wavefunction in an atom.
A mathematical function used to calculate detection probabilities.
Labels specifying properties of allowed quantum states.
A measurable quantity associated with rotation or spin.

The small central part of an atom containing its proton or protons.
A unit of an element made of a nucleus and electrons.

quantum-hydrogen-and-orbitals.question: What does the direction-independent 1s probability pattern tell you?
choices: At the same distance from the center, detection probability density is the same in every direction.
The electron follows a fixed circular path.
The electron must be found in one preferred direction.
quantum-hydrogen-and-orbitals.feedback: The 1s probability pattern is spherical: at a given distance from the center, no direction is preferred. It is a probability pattern, not a fixed path.
quantum-hydrogen-and-orbitals.practice: Describe the difference between an orbital probability picture and a path around the nucleus.

quantum-identical-particles.title: Identical Particles
explanation: Two electrons are identical particles: exchanging their labels does not create a physically different kind of particle. Quantum descriptions must account for this. Electrons belong to a group called fermions. The Pauli exclusion principle says that identical fermions cannot occupy the same complete single-particle state. This affects how electrons fill the available states in atoms.

An orbital describes only the spatial part of an electron’s state. It can hold two electrons with different spin states. A third electron cannot share that same orbital if it would duplicate one of those complete states. Another group, bosons, does not follow this exclusion restriction. Photons, the particles of light, are bosons; many can occupy the same state. Particle identity therefore changes which arrangements are allowed.
quantum-identical-particles.example: An atom’s 1s orbital already contains two electrons with opposite spin states. A third electron must use another available state rather than becoming a third electron in that orbital.

terms.definition: Particles of the same type whose exchange does not make them physically distinguishable.

quantum-identical-particles.question: Where must a third electron go when 1s already holds two electrons?
choices: Into the same 1s orbital with identical spin
quantum-identical-particles.feedback: The two allowed spin states in that orbital are already occupied, so the third electron needs another state.
quantum-identical-particles.practice: Draw one orbital with two boxes for its spin states. Fill both, then show where an extra electron must go.

University of California, San Diego: Identical particles

quantum-approximation-methods.title: Approximation Methods
explanation: Many quantum problems are too complicated to solve exactly with a short formula. An approximation gives a useful estimate while keeping track of what was simplified. Perturbation theory starts with a model we can solve, then adds corrections for a small extra effect. It works best when that extra effect is small enough for the corrections to stay under control.

The variational method tries different allowed wavefunctions and compares their average energies. For the lowest-energy state, these trial energies cannot fall below the exact lowest energy if the method is applied correctly. A lower trial value is a better energy estimate, but does not guarantee every detail is right. Good approximations are checked by improving the calculation, comparing methods, or comparing predictions with experiments.
quantum-approximation-methods.example: Suppose two valid trial wavefunctions give lowest-energy estimates of 8 and 6 units. The estimate of 6 gives the tighter upper bound, though the exact energy may be lower.

terms.definition: A calculation designed to be close enough while simplifying a problem.
A method adding small corrections to a solvable starting model.
A method varying trial states to improve energy estimates.
A function used to calculate quantum measurement probabilities.
The expected average across many energy measurements on the same prepared state.
A value that the true quantity cannot exceed.
An allowed candidate wavefunction used in an estimate.
Relating to the physical description used for systems such as atoms and electrons.

quantum-approximation-methods.question: Which valid trial gives the tighter upper bound on the lowest energy?
choices: Both must equal the exact energy
quantum-approximation-methods.feedback: Six is the lower valid upper bound. It gets closer from above, but may still differ from the exact value.
quantum-approximation-methods.practice: Explain one reason to check an approximation against a more detailed calculation.

quantum-density-matrices.title: Density Matrices
explanation: A density matrix is a square table of numbers used to describe a quantum state. It can describe a pure state, including a superposition, or a mixed state. A mixed state can arise when we randomly prepare different states or consider one part of a larger entangled system. The table lets us calculate measurement probabilities in each case.

For a qubit written in the 0-and-1 arrangement, the diagonal entries give the chances of those measurement answers. Other entries carry information about coherence: phase relationships that can affect interference. Equal 0-or-1 chances do not make two density matrices identical. A coherent plus state and an equal random mixture of 0 and 1 both give 50–50 in that measurement, but can respond differently when an operation comes before measurement.
quantum-density-matrices.example: Apply a Hadamard gate to either preparation. The ideal plus state then gives 0 for sure; the equal random mixture still gives 0 or 1 with equal chance.

terms.definition: A square table representing a quantum state and predicting its measurement results.
A quantum state represented by one state vector.
A state that cannot be described by a single pure-state vector.
A quantum system with two reference states.
Entries along the line from a table’s top left to its bottom right.
Phase relationships allowing amplitudes to interfere.
An equal coherent combination of 0 and 1 with matching phases.
An operation that converts the plus state to 0 and 0 to the plus state.
Having a joint quantum state that cannot be written as a random mixture of independent part states.
A list of amplitudes describing a pure quantum state.
A quantity describing how amplitudes combine.
Amplitudes combining to strengthen or cancel outcomes.
A number used to calculate a quantum outcome’s chance.

quantum-density-matrices.question: Which preparation gives definitely 0 after the ideal Hadamard gate?
quantum-density-matrices.feedback: The plus state retains the phase relationship needed to combine into 0. The random mixture does not.
quantum-density-matrices.practice: Explain why a list containing only 50% for 0 and 50% for 1 can leave out quantum information.

quantum-entanglement-and-correlations.title: Entanglement and Correlations
explanation: A correlation means results from two systems are related. For example, two matching cards have correlated colors. Entanglement is a stronger kind of quantum relationship: the joint state cannot be described as independent states of the parts, even after allowing a random mixture of such independent preparations. Some correlations are ordinary; correlation alone does not prove entanglement.

Consider a pair of qubits in the Bell plus state. Measuring both in the usual 0-or-1 arrangement gives either 00 or 11, with equal chance. Each person’s individual answer is random, but their answers match. Matching alone could also come from ordinary shared randomness. Testing other measurement arrangements reveals the special quantum relationship. Neither person can choose their random outcome to send an instant message. Comparing the recorded results requires ordinary communication.
quantum-entanglement-and-correlations.example: In one Bell-pair trial, Ana gets 1 and Ben gets 1. Their matching answer fits the prediction, but that single matching pair does not establish entanglement by itself.

terms.definition: A relationship between results or quantities.
A joint state that cannot be written as a random mixture of independent part states.
A quantum system with reference states 0 and 1.
An equal coherent combination of the pair states 00 and 11.
The description of two or more systems considered together.
The chosen physical setup and states distinguished by a measurement.

quantum-entanglement-and-correlations.question: What can Ana and Ben conclude from one matching answer?
choices: It fits the prediction but does not alone prove entanglement
quantum-entanglement-and-correlations.feedback: Ordinary shared randomness can also produce matching answers. Other measurements and repeated trials are needed.
quantum-entanglement-and-correlations.practice: Compare matching cards with a Bell pair. Explain why matching in just one measurement arrangement is not enough.
