IBM Quantum: Quantum information for multiple systems

quantum-decoherence-and-noise.title: Decoherence and Noise
explanation: Coherence means a quantum state retains phase relationships that allow interference. A system can lose observable coherence when it interacts with its environment and becomes linked with it. If we do not track that environment, the system’s interference can shrink or disappear. This process is called decoherence. It does not require a person watching or deciding anything.

Noise means unwanted changes or errors in a quantum experiment. It can include loss of coherence, loss of energy, and incorrect recorded answers. These effects matter because a circuit relies on carefully controlled state changes. Keeping systems well isolated and improving controls can reduce some noise. Repeating an experiment helps reveal error patterns, but repeating alone does not restore the state’s lost phase information.
quantum-decoherence-and-noise.example: Ideally, two Hadamard gates in a row return a qubit from 0 to 0. If unwanted environmental interactions occur between them, repeated trials can include 1 results instead.

terms.definition: Phase relationships that allow quantum amplitudes to interfere.
A quantity controlling how an amplitude combines with others.
Amplitudes combining to strengthen or cancel outcomes.
Surroundings that can interact with the system.
Loss of observable phase relationships when the environment is not tracked.
Unwanted changes or errors affecting a quantum experiment.
A sequence of operations and measurements.
A quantum system with reference states 0 and 1.
An operation that converts 0 to the plus state and the plus state back to 0.
A number used to calculate a quantum outcome’s chance.
An equal superposition of 0 and 1 with matching phases.
A combination of reference states with amplitudes.

quantum-decoherence-and-noise.question: Why might the two-gate experiment produce some 1 results?
choices: A person must have thought about 1
Unwanted interactions can spoil the controlled state changes
quantum-decoherence-and-noise.feedback: Noise between the gates can change the state, including the phase information needed for the ideal return to 0.
quantum-decoherence-and-noise.practice: Name one unwanted interaction a laboratory might try to reduce, such as nearby electrical signals.

quantum-quantum-information.title: Quantum Information
explanation: A quantum circuit is a step-by-step plan for preparing states, applying gates, and making measurements. Its information is carried by qubits. A gate changes the state in a controlled way. Some gates act on one qubit; others connect the behavior of several. A measurement gives an ordinary recorded result that a regular computer can store and use.

What makes a circuit useful is how its operations combine amplitudes before the final measurement. They can increase the chances of useful answers and reduce others through interference. Measuring does not reveal every amplitude or every possible answer at once. A useful quantum algorithm must arrange the circuit so its limited recorded results help solve the particular task. Quantum computers do not automatically solve every problem faster than ordinary computers.
quantum-quantum-information.example: Start an ideal qubit at 0. Apply a Hadamard gate, then measure: 0 and 1 are equally likely. Apply two Hadamard gates before measuring instead: the result is 0.

terms.definition: A sequence of state preparations, gates, and measurements.
A quantum system with reference states 0 and 1.
A controlled operation that changes a quantum state.
A number used to calculate an outcome’s chance.
Amplitudes combining to strengthen or cancel outcomes.
A sequence of steps for completing a task.
An operation that turns 0 into an equal superposition and reverses that change when applied again.
A combination of reference states with probability amplitudes.
A mathematical description used to predict a quantum system’s measurement results.

quantum-quantum-information.question: What is the ideal result after two Hadamard gates starting from 0?
quantum-quantum-information.feedback: The second gate reverses the first in this ideal circuit, returning the state to 0.
quantum-quantum-information.practice: Draw two circuit plans: one gate then measurement, and two gates then measurement. Label the predicted results.

art-line-control.title: Line Control
explanation: Line control means choosing the marks you make. A line can be straight, curved, long, short, thick, or thin. Its direction also matters: it can travel across the page, up and down, or diagonally. With a pencil, lighter pressure usually produces a lighter mark. More pressure usually makes it darker, though the pencil and paper affect the result.

Before drawing a line, look at its starting and ending points. Move your hand through the motion just above the paper, then make the mark. Try one clear stroke and notice what happened. If it bends when you wanted it straight, adjust your movement on the next attempt. Practicing control means learning which motion and pressure produce the mark you intended; it does not mean every drawing needs perfectly straight lines.
art-line-control.example: Draw a leaf with a light curved edge and a darker central line. The two marks have different jobs, so choose their pressure deliberately.

terms.definition: Making deliberate choices about a line’s direction, shape, and weight.
How firmly you press a drawing tool onto the surface.
One movement of a drawing tool that leaves a mark.
Slanting rather than horizontal or vertical.
The thickness or visual strength of a line.
Running left to right, parallel to a level ground line.
Running straight up and down.

art-line-control.question: How could you make the leaf’s central line darker with the same pencil?
art-line-control.feedback: More pencil pressure usually darkens the mark. Test gently because the tool and paper also matter.
art-line-control.practice: Make five straight lines and five curves. Repeat them with light and firmer pressure, then circle one intentional mark.

sources.title: National Gallery of Art: Drawing basics

art-observational-sketching.title: Observational Sketching
explanation: Observational sketching means making a quick drawing while looking carefully at a real object or a reference picture. Your job is to notice what is visible. Look at the whole object first. Is it taller than it is wide? Where does it bend? Which parts overlap? Draw the largest shapes lightly before adding details, and keep looking back at the subject.

Then compare one clear feature at a time. Check the top, bottom, widest point, or the space inside a handle. If the sketch differs, name the difference precisely: “My cup is wider than the reference.” That gives you a useful next change. You do not need to judge the entire drawing as good or bad. A visible difference can teach you what to look at more closely.
art-observational-sketching.example: Your reference mug looks twice as tall as it is wide, but your sketch is nearly a square. Narrowing the sketch would bring its overall shape closer to the reference.

terms.definition: A quick drawing made by looking closely at a subject.
The object or picture you use to guide a drawing.
One part covering some of another part from your viewpoint.
The large outer shape before small details are added.

art-observational-sketching.question: What change would help this mug sketch match the reference?
art-observational-sketching.feedback: The reference is tall and narrow. Reducing the drawn width improves that large relationship.
art-observational-sketching.practice: Sketch a spoon for two minutes. Compare its length, widest part, and handle curve with the real spoon.

sources.title: National Gallery of Art: Drawing everyday objects

art-simple-shapes.title: Simple Shapes
explanation: Complicated objects become easier to draw when you begin with a few simple shapes. A shape is flat: it has height and width. Circles, ovals, rectangles, and triangles are useful starting points. Look for the largest shape first, then add smaller shapes for its parts. These are light planning marks, so you can move or resize them before drawing the final edges.

The shapes do not need to describe every detail. A shoe might begin as a long oval, with a smaller shape for the heel. After checking their sizes and positions, adjust the outline to match the actual shoe. The simple shapes help you organize what you see. They are a starting plan, rather than a demand that every natural object fit a geometric shape.
art-simple-shapes.example: A toy car can begin with a long rectangle for the body, a smaller rectangle for the cabin, and two circles for the visible wheels. Curved corners come later.
art-simple-shapes.analogy: Simple shapes work like temporary building pieces for a drawing. They help with placement, but you still adjust them to match what you actually see.

terms.definition: A flat area with height and width.
A rounded shape longer in one direction.
A four-sided shape with four right angles.
The line around a visible outer edge.
A shape described by regular mathematical relationships, such as a circle or square.
An angle of 90 degrees, like the corner of a square.

art-simple-shapes.question: Which plan fits the toy car in the example?
choices: A body rectangle, cabin rectangle, and wheel circles
art-simple-shapes.feedback: Those large shapes match the main visible parts and make their placement easier to check.
art-simple-shapes.practice: Choose a backpack, shoe, or kettle. Draw three to five light shapes, then adjust them into the object’s outline.

art-basic-proportion.title: Basic Proportion
explanation: Proportion means the size of one part compared with another. A handle might be half as tall as a cup, or a window might be one-quarter as wide as a wall. These comparisons help you draw a subject at any size. Instead of asking only, “How big is the handle?” ask, “How big is it compared with the cup?”

Check placement too. Notice where a part starts, where it ends, and how much space separates it from other parts. Begin with the whole subject’s height and width, then compare the smaller parts. Use your reference rather than assuming every similar object has the same proportions. You can also change proportions on purpose, but first notice which relationship you are changing and how it affects the result.
art-basic-proportion.example: A reference cup is 8 units tall and its handle is 4 units tall. If you draw the cup 6 centimeters tall, a 3-centimeter handle keeps that height relationship.

terms.definition: The size of one part compared with another.
An object or picture used to guide a drawing.
Size described by comparison with something else.
Where a part is positioned in the drawing.

art-basic-proportion.question: How tall should the handle be for the 6-centimeter cup?
art-basic-proportion.feedback: The handle is half the cup’s height. Half of 6 centimeters is 3 centimeters.
art-basic-proportion.practice: Draw a bottle twice. Make the second drawing smaller while keeping its cap, neck, and body in the same proportions.

art-perspective-basics.title: Perspective Basics
explanation: Perspective helps a flat drawing suggest depth. In one-point perspective, begin with a horizon line representing your eye level and a vanishing point on that line. Lines that are parallel in the scene and head directly away from you appear to approach that point. This is why the sides of a straight hallway seem to come together in the distance.

Draw the near face of a box. From its corners, lightly draw lines toward the vanishing point, then choose where the back of the box ends. In this simple setup, the front’s horizontal and vertical edges keep their directions. Do not send every line to the point: only the set heading away from you uses it. Objects of equal real size generally appear smaller as they get farther away.
art-perspective-basics.example: In a straight hallway drawing, the floor’s left and right edges approach the same vanishing point. The nearby doorway is larger on the page than an equally sized distant doorway.

terms.definition: Drawing methods that suggest depth and a viewpoint.
A setup in which one set of receding parallel lines approaches one vanishing point.
The line representing the viewer’s eye level.
A point where a set of receding parallel lines appears to meet.
Running in the same direction without meeting in the real scene.
Going farther away from the viewer.
Running left to right, parallel to a level ground line.
Running straight up and down.

art-perspective-basics.question: Which lines approach the hallway’s vanishing point?
choices: Every line, including a nearby vertical door edge
art-perspective-basics.feedback: The floor edges belong to the parallel set heading into the distance in this one-point setup.
art-perspective-basics.practice: Draw a horizon, one vanishing point, and a simple box below the horizon. Keep the guide lines light.

art-light-and-shadow.title: Light and Shadow
explanation: Light and shadow tell us which way a surface faces and where objects sit. First find the light source: a lamp, window, or the Sun. Surfaces facing the source generally receive more light. Surfaces turned away receive less. A cast shadow forms on another surface when the object blocks light. That is different from the dark side of the object itself.

For a drawing with one strong light, keep its direction consistent. If the lamp is on the left, the cast shadow usually extends away from it toward the right across the table. Observe the shadow’s actual shape before drawing it. Its size and softness depend on the light, object, and receiving surface. You can test the setup by moving a lamp and watching how the shadow changes.
art-light-and-shadow.example: A ball sits on a table with a lamp above and to the left. Its upper-left area is bright, and its cast shadow falls across the table to the right.

terms.definition: Something that emits light, such as a lamp or the Sun.
A dark area on another surface where an object blocks light.
The darker part of an object turned away from the light.
Marks used to show areas of light and dark.

art-light-and-shadow.question: Where should the example’s cast shadow mainly extend?
choices: Away from the lamp toward the right
Toward the lamp on the left
art-light-and-shadow.feedback: The ball blocks the lamp’s light, so the shadow extends away from the lamp across the table.
art-light-and-shadow.practice: Place a cup under one lamp. Sketch the cup and its cast shadow, then move the lamp and sketch again.

sources.title: Smithsonian: The science of light and shadows

art-form-in-space.title: Form in Space
explanation: A shape is flat, while a form has height, width, and depth. A circle can suggest a ball when you add shading that follows its rounded surface. A rectangle can suggest a box when you add visible side and top faces. Think about which surfaces point toward the light and which turn away, then use lighter and darker marks to show that change.

Overlap also helps show space. When one object covers part of another, we usually read it as being in front. Combine that clear placement clue with consistent shading. You do not need to darken every edge equally. Look for where a boundary is sharp and where a curved surface changes gradually from light to dark. These choices can help the viewer understand the form without many small details.
art-form-in-space.example: Draw a shaded ball partly covering a box. The overlap places the ball in front, while the light-to-dark change helps it appear rounded rather than like a flat circle.

terms.definition: A flat area with height and width.
A three-dimensional object, or its appearance in a drawing.
Having height, width, and depth.
Marks showing differences in light and dark.
How light or dark an area is.
One object covering part of another from the viewer’s position.

art-form-in-space.question: What shows that the ball is in front of the box?
choices: Every edge having the same darkness
Its overlap covering part of the box
art-form-in-space.feedback: The covered part of the box provides a clear depth clue: the ball sits between the viewer and the box.
art-form-in-space.practice: Draw a circle beside a shaded ball. Add a box behind the ball and explain the two depth clues you used.

sources.title: Getty: Exploring value to create form

art-texture-studies.title: Texture Studies
explanation: Texture describes how a surface feels, such as rough, smooth, soft, or bumpy. A drawing can suggest texture using marks even though the paper itself has a different feel. Look for repeated surface features: fur has strands, stone may have cracks, and a woven cloth has crossing threads. Choose a few marks that communicate the most useful feature.

The marks should follow the surface. Short lines on a furry round object can curve around its shape instead of all pointing straight down. Leave some areas quieter so the larger shape stays clear. You do not have to copy every hair or crack. Try a small sample patch first, compare it with your reference, and adjust the spacing, direction, or darkness of the marks.
art-texture-studies.example: Draw two equal squares. Fill one with irregular short cracks to suggest rough stone. Fill the other with long, gently curving strands to suggest fur. Their outlines match, but their surfaces look different.

terms.definition: The surface quality something has or appears to have.
Marks that suggest how a depicted surface would feel.
An object or picture used to guide a drawing.
The distance between repeated marks.
A thin length of material, such as one hair.

art-texture-studies.question: What mainly makes the two squares suggest different materials?
art-texture-studies.feedback: The cracks and strands provide different visual texture clues even though the squares have equal size.
art-texture-studies.practice: Make three small texture patches for bark, cloth, and a smooth pebble. Use a different mark pattern for each.

art-gesture-and-rhythm.title: Gesture and Rhythm
explanation: A gesture drawing is a quick sketch of a subject’s overall action. Before drawing small details, notice the tilt of the body, the direction of the limbs, and where the weight seems to rest. Use a few long lines and simple shapes to capture those relationships. A line of action is a planning line that follows the pose’s main bend or movement.

Rhythm in drawing comes from repeating or connecting marks and shapes in a way that carries the eye through the picture. In a figure, related curves can help the arms, torso, and legs feel connected. Speed helps you focus on the whole pose, but rushing blindly does not help. Look first, make a few marks, and check whether they show the action. Details can come after the main pose is clear.
art-gesture-and-rhythm.example: A person reaches up for a shelf. A rising curved line through the torso, a lifted shoulder, and an extended arm show the reach before you draw fingers or clothing.

terms.definition: A quick drawing focused on overall shape, pose, or action.
A planning line showing a pose’s main direction or bend.
Repeating or related visual elements that suggest movement through a picture.
The main body area between the neck and hips.
The position of a person’s body.

art-gesture-and-rhythm.question: What should you draw first to show the example’s reach?
choices: The torso’s rise and the extended arm
art-gesture-and-rhythm.feedback: Those large relationships communicate the action. Small details can wait until the reach is clear.
art-gesture-and-rhythm.practice: Use three clothed reference poses. Spend 30 seconds on each, drawing only the main action and limb directions.

sources.title: National Gallery of Art: Drawing basics

art-figure-anatomy.title: Figure Anatomy
explanation: Anatomy means the structure of the body. For a first figure drawing, begin with the major parts: head, rib cage, pelvis, arms, and legs. You can use simple rounded forms and blocks to plan them. These shapes help you see their sizes, angles, and connections before adding the body’s outer edges. They are drawing tools, so adjust them to the person you observe.

Joints connect bones and allow movement. Mark shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles so the limbs bend in sensible places. Watch how the rib cage and pelvis tilt relative to each other. A raised arm affects the shoulder, and a bent knee changes the leg’s direction. People differ in size and proportion; use the actual reference rather than treating one standard figure as every human body.
art-figure-anatomy.example: For a seated person, draw the rib cage above the pelvis, then thighs angling toward the knees and lower legs leading to the feet. Place each bend at a joint.

terms.definition: The structure of a body and its parts.
The ribs and breastbone around the chest.
The bony structure at the hips.
A place where bones connect.
A shape understood as having height, width, and depth.
The size of one part compared with another.
The person or image you look at while drawing.
The part of a leg between the hip and knee.

art-figure-anatomy.question: Where should the seated person’s leg change direction between thigh and lower leg?
choices: At a random place halfway along the thigh
art-figure-anatomy.feedback: The knee connects the thigh and lower leg, so that is where this bend belongs.
art-figure-anatomy.practice: Sketch a clothed seated figure using six main forms and dots for joints. Compare its bends with the reference.

art-composition-and-focus.title: Composition and Focus
explanation: Composition is how you arrange everything inside a picture. Before adding detail, choose what you want the viewer to notice first. That area is the focal point. You can draw attention with a clear shape, an unusual size, a strong light-and-dark difference, or a different color. The strongest difference does not have to sit in the exact center.

Look at the other areas too. If every object has equally strong detail and contrast, they may compete for attention. Try making the surroundings quieter, then check whether your chosen subject stands out. A tiny rough sketch can test the arrangement quickly. Move, resize, or simplify shapes until the picture supports your goal. These are useful choices, rather than a formula that every drawing must follow.
art-composition-and-focus.example: You want a white lighthouse to stand out against a dark hill. Give that area the clearest light-and-dark contrast, while making the nearby small houses less detailed and closer in value.

terms.definition: The arrangement of elements inside a picture.
The area you want the viewer to notice first.
A noticeable difference, such as light beside dark.
How light or dark an area is.
Drawing attention to one part of a design.
The person, object, or place a drawing focuses on.

art-composition-and-focus.question: Which change would support the lighthouse as the focal point?
choices: Hide the lighthouse behind the hill
Make every house equally bright and detailed
Give the lighthouse the clearest contrast
art-composition-and-focus.feedback: A clear contrast helps attract attention there, while quieter surroundings reduce competition.
art-composition-and-focus.practice: Make two tiny lighthouse sketches. Change its position and surrounding dark shapes, then choose the clearer arrangement.

art-portrait-structure.title: Portrait Structure
explanation: A portrait shows a particular person. Begin by observing the whole head’s shape and tilt. Draw it lightly, then add a centerline showing the direction the face points. Place guide lines for the eyes, nose, and mouth according to the reference. These lines help the features belong to one head rather than looking like separate pieces pasted onto the page.

Compare distances before drawing eyelashes or individual hairs. How far are the eyes from the chin? How wide is the mouth compared with the nose? Turning or tilting a head changes how those relationships appear on the page. Common proportion guides can help you start, but faces differ. Keep returning to the actual person. Check one relationship at a time and make small changes while the marks are still light.
art-portrait-structure.example: In a turned-head reference, one side of the face appears narrower. Drawing both sides equally wide would change the apparent direction. Adjusting the centerline and visible widths helps show the turn.

terms.definition: An artwork showing a particular person.
A planning line marking the middle direction of the face.
A light temporary line used to place parts.
The size or spacing of parts compared with each other.
The person or picture used to guide the drawing.
A part of the face, such as an eye, nose, or mouth.

art-portrait-structure.question: What helps show the head turning in this example?
choices: Adjusting the centerline and side widths to match the reference
art-portrait-structure.feedback: A turn changes the visible shape and widths. Those larger relationships matter before small details.
art-portrait-structure.practice: Draw a head shape and place only the eyes, nose, and mouth. Name one spacing you checked against the reference.

art-complex-scene-planning.title: Complex Scene Planning
explanation: A complex scene becomes easier to draw when you plan its large parts first. Make a thumbnail: a small, quick sketch that tests the arrangement. Divide the scene into foreground, middle ground, and background. These names describe the parts that appear nearest, farther away, and farthest away. You do not need a hard dividing line between them.

Choose the main subject, then place the largest shapes around it. Check what overlaps, which objects need space, and how the viewer’s attention can reach the subject. Try two or three thumbnails before choosing one. Change the arrangement while it is small and simple. Once the plan is clear, enlarge it and add details. A good plan leaves enough room for important parts instead of discovering too late that a building or person will not fit.
art-complex-scene-planning.example: Plan a park with a nearby bench in the foreground, a person beside a tree in the middle ground, and distant buildings in the background. Let the bench partly overlap the tree’s base.

terms.definition: A small, rough sketch used to test a picture’s arrangement.
The part of a scene that appears nearest to the viewer.
The part between the nearest and farthest areas.
The part that appears farthest away.
One object covering part of another from the viewer’s position.
The arrangement of elements inside a picture.

art-complex-scene-planning.question: Which part of the planned park is in the foreground?
art-complex-scene-planning.feedback: The bench is closest to the viewer in this plan, so it belongs to the foreground.
art-complex-scene-planning.practice: Make three small park thumbnails. Change the bench position, then choose one where the person remains easy to see.

art-materials-and-surface.title: Materials and Surface
explanation: You can suggest different materials by changing both surface marks and edges. An edge is where one visible area meets another. A sharp edge changes suddenly; a soft edge changes gradually. Observe how light looks on the material before deciding which marks to use. A polished metal cup may show crisp bright reflections, while folded cloth often shows broader changes between light and dark.

Texture and lighting work together. Wood grain can suggest a wooden surface, but its light and shadow must still follow the object’s shape. Avoid covering everything with the same pattern. Test a small patch for each material, then choose the marks that best match your reference. Keep enough clear light and dark areas for the whole form to read. Some materials change appearance strongly with lighting, so their marks are not fixed recipes.
art-materials-and-surface.example: Draw a shiny spoon next to a cloth napkin. Use clear narrow light shapes on the spoon and broader shaded folds on the napkin, checking both against the same light source.

terms.definition: The substance an object is made from, such as metal, wood, or cloth.
The boundary where visible areas meet.
A boundary with a sudden change.
A boundary with a gradual change.
Light redirected from a surface.
The surface quality something has or appears to have.
The visible pattern formed by wood’s structure.
The object or image used to guide a drawing.
Marks showing the light and dark areas of a surface.

art-materials-and-surface.question: Which choice helps distinguish the example’s spoon from the napkin?
choices: Use the same folds and marks on both
Use observed crisp reflections on the spoon and shaded folds on the cloth
art-materials-and-surface.feedback: Their different light patterns and surface clues help suggest metal and cloth.
art-materials-and-surface.practice: Draw two small patches from nearby materials. Name one edge difference and one surface-mark difference.

art-color-and-atmosphere.title: Color and Atmosphere
explanation: Color can support a scene’s mood and help suggest distance. Begin with a limited palette: a small set of colors chosen for the drawing. Reusing those colors can connect different areas. Try a few colored patches before filling the page. Notice their value, meaning how light or dark they are, as well as the color itself. Different colors can still have similar values.

Atmospheric perspective describes how distant objects can look less distinct because we view them through more air. In many landscapes, faraway hills have less light-and-dark contrast and appear lighter or bluer than nearby ones. Look at the actual scene, because weather and lighting can change the effect. Color can suggest a feeling, but there is no single color that makes every viewer feel exactly the same thing.
art-color-and-atmosphere.example: For a quiet misty landscape, choose blue, gray, and a little green. Give the distant hill lighter values and softer differences than the nearby dark tree, so their distances are easier to read.

terms.definition: The set of colors chosen for an artwork.
How light or dark a color or area is.
Suggesting distance through changes in clarity, contrast, and often color.
A noticeable difference between neighboring areas.
The feeling a scene suggests to a viewer.

art-color-and-atmosphere.question: Which choice helps the example’s hill appear farther away?
choices: Use lighter values and weaker contrast
Give every area the same dark outline
Make its details stronger than the nearby tree’s
art-color-and-atmosphere.feedback: Reduced contrast and lighter values can suggest distance through mist in this particular scene.
art-color-and-atmosphere.practice: Draw three hill shapes using a small palette. Make the farthest hill lighter and lower in contrast than the nearest.

art-finished-drawing-project.title: Finished Drawing Project
explanation: A finished drawing grows from a clear plan and a few deliberate choices. Pick a subject and a goal you can explain, such as making a cup look rounded or showing a person reading beside a window. Make a small planning sketch, choose your materials, and decide where the drawing’s light and dark areas will go. Begin lightly so you can adjust the large shapes.

Develop the whole drawing before spending too long on one tiny area. Check sizes, placement, and lighting, then add the details that support your goal. Pause and look from a little farther away. Ask whether the main subject is clear and whether anything needs changing. Finishing does not require filling every space. You decide when the drawing communicates what you intended, then describe the choices that helped it do so.
art-finished-drawing-project.example: You draw a mug beside an apple. You adjust their relative sizes, add a cast shadow from one lamp, and leave the background simple so the two objects remain easy to notice.

terms.definition: A quick drawing used to prepare a larger work.
The tool or substance used to make art, such as pencil or charcoal.
Size compared with something else in the picture.
A dark area on a surface where an object blocks light.
The arrangement of elements inside a picture.
How light or dark an area is.
A carbon drawing material used to make dark marks.

art-finished-drawing-project.question: Which explanation clearly describes a useful choice in the example?
choices: “It is good because I say so.”
“I left the background simple so the mug and apple stand out.”
“Every square of paper must be filled.”
art-finished-drawing-project.feedback: That explanation connects a visible drawing choice with its purpose.
art-finished-drawing-project.practice: Finish a drawing of two everyday objects. Write two sentences explaining one change you made and why you made it.
